contents.html: This report presents the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 requirements for exchanging biometric and forensic data using a machine-readable specification (MRS) that allows software tools to process the requirements directly. NIST developed a modular JSON architecture and an automated build process to manage, validate, and transform the MRS data using a proof-of-concept HTML specification directly from the JSON source. It demonstrates how the MRS can augment the base standard for developers, testers, and auditors to lower adoption barriers, reduce interpretation gaps, and provide a maintained digital companion to the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 specification.
contents.html_ja: この報告書は、ソフトウェアツールが要件を直接処理できる機械可読仕様（MRS）を用いて、バイオメトリクスデータおよび法科学データを交換するための ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 の要件を示します。NIST は、モジュール式の JSON アーキテクチャと自動ビルドプロセスを開発し、MRS データを管理、検証、変換するとともに、JSON ソースから直接、概念実証用の HTML 仕様を生成しました。この報告書は、MRS が基本規格を開発者、試験者、監査者向けに補完し、導入障壁を下げ、解釈のずれを減らし、ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 仕様を補う、継続的に保守されるデジタル資料を提供できることを示します。

contents.html: The first version of the ANSI/NBS-ICST 1-1986 standard was published by NIST (then the National Bureau of Standards) in 1986 as a 53-page document. That version focused exclusively on fingerprint identification and a data format for information exchange between organizations. Since then, the standard has evolved to meet the needs of national and international law enforcement and biometric organizations by incorporating new biometric modalities, encoding formats, and metadata fields.
contents.html_ja: ANSI/NBS-ICST 1-1986 規格の最初の版は、1986年に NIST（当時の米国標準局）により、53 ページの文書として刊行されました。その版は、指紋の識別と、組織間で情報を交換するためのデータ形式だけに焦点を当てていました。それ以来、この規格は、新しいバイオメトリクスのモダリティ、エンコーディング形式、メタデータフィールドを取り込みながら、国内外の法執行機関およびバイオメトリクス関連組織のニーズに応えるべく進化してきました。

contents.html: ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025, Data Format for the Interchange of Fingerprint, Facial and Other Biometric Information [1], is the latest revision of the global standard for biometric and forensic data. It has expanded to include guidance and data format specifications for various biometric modalities, including facial, iris, plantar, and DNA data. As the number of modalities and the complexity of the information have increased over time, the specification has grown to exceed 600 pages. Traditionally, software developers and system integrators have used this standard as a text-based reference, manually extracting and interpreting technical requirements to develop conformant software.
contents.html_ja: ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025『Data Format for the Interchange of Fingerprint, Facial and Other Biometric Information』[1] は、バイオメトリクスデータおよび法科学データに関する国際規格の最新の改訂版です。この規格は、顔、虹彩、足底、DNA のデータなど、さまざまなバイオメトリクスのモダリティに関するガイダンスとデータ形式の仕様を含むよう拡張されてきました。モダリティの数と情報の複雑さが時間とともに増すにつれ、仕様は 600 ページを超えるまでに大きくなりました。従来、ソフトウェア開発者とシステムインテグレーターは、この規格をテキストベースの参考資料として用い、技術的要件を手作業で抽出・解釈して、適合したソフトウェアを開発してきました。

contents.html: The ANSI/NIST-ITL 1 standards have historically required extensive cross-referencing within the document. Requirements for a single data element (e.g., data type, character constraints, occurrence limits) are often distributed and repeated across narrative sections and associated tables. This fragmentation has increased the risk of ambiguity when separate sections present inconsistent or conflicting guidance, particularly in a long and complex technical specification maintained over multiple revisions. Organizations have therefore had to reconcile related requirements before implementing them, and independent reconciliation efforts could lead to divergent interpretations and subtle interoperability challenges.

contents.html: NIST developed a JSON-encoded version of ANSI/NIST-ITL 1 to provide the global community with a single shared interpretation of the standard’s complex requirements. The MRS facilitates rapid, consistent, and accurate deployments of the standard across varied technical environments and supports the exchange and integrity of biometric and forensic transactions. It can be used directly by software and adapted into implementation profiles to help minimize interoperability issues between organizations, ensure that disparate systems remain consistent and reduce the resource-intensive nature of manual requirement extraction. This will also enable NIST and the biometric community to manage the complexity of biometric data format requirements with greater agility, including simplified auditing and the integration of community contributions (e.g., corrections, enhancements). By providing a consistent digital reference, this machine-readable representation can be reliably deployed across multiple organizations to support the implementation of the standard.

contents.html: Beyond structural mirroring, the JSON schema incorporates a logic-handling system to manage the standard’s complex requirements. It uses specialized definitions for condition and occurrence types that allow for encoding specific rules. For example, a field may be mandatory in a traditional encoding but optional in a National Information Exchange Model (NIEM) (i.e., XML-based) encoding. These logic structures (including predicates, outcomes, and Boolean operations; see Appendix A.2) are integrated directly into the data elements. This enables the representation of conditional dependencies, where the requirements for a specific field are contingent upon the value of a separate data element. For example, the Value Constraints for field 8.006 (seen at the bottom of Fig. 1) are governed by the value of the Scan Resolution Table (SRT) field. In this example, SRT values 0 and 1 require field 8.006 to contain an integer from 10 to 65535, while SRT value 2 requires the field value to be 0. The following JSON fragment, summarized in Fig. 2, provides an example of how these conditional value constraints are formalized. Appendix B Fig. 8 provides the complete JSON data for field 8.006.

contents.html: NIST developed a strongly typed JSON schema and a suite of Python scripts to aggregate, validate, and transform the data in the MRS. Python was selected for this effort because of its widespread availability across numerous platforms as well as its extensive and mature libraries for JSON processing and data validation. This ensures that the tools remain accessible to the biometric community and can effectively manage the structural complexities of the MRS.

contents.html: The MRS is maintained as modular partial JSON files rather than as one monolithic document. The complete MRS is nearly 120,000 lines, and a single file proved difficult to edit in common development environments. The partial files are development modules; the build process assembles them into a complete JSON document for validation and publication. This modular structure also supports implementation profiles that include only records, fields, or other data relevant to a specific deployment.

contents.html: The MRS for ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 translates text-based biometric data exchange requirements into structured JSON. By converting more than 600 pages of requirements into machine-processable data, NIST has reduced the need for manual extraction and lowered the risk of inconsistent interpretation. This project uses modular JSON files, a JSON schema, and automated build scripts to assemble and validate the MRS. NIST expert review remains necessary to ensure that the JSON accurately represents the base standard.

This report presents the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 requirements for exchanging biometric and forensic data using a machine-readable specification (MRS) that allows software tools to process the requirements directly. NIST developed a modular JSON architecture and an automated build process to manage, validate, and transform the MRS data using a proof-of-concept HTML specification directly from the JSON source. It demonstrates how the MRS can augment the base standard for developers, testers, and auditors to lower adoption barriers, reduce interpretation gaps, and provide a maintained digital companion to the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 specification.

The first version of the ANSI/NBS-ICST 1-1986 standard was published by NIST (then the National Bureau of Standards) in 1986 as a 53-page document. That version focused exclusively on fingerprint identification and a data format for information exchange between organizations. Since then, the standard has evolved to meet the needs of national and international law enforcement and biometric organizations by incorporating new biometric modalities, encoding formats, and metadata fields.

ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025, Data Format for the Interchange of Fingerprint, Facial and Other Biometric Information [1], is the latest revision of the global standard for biometric and forensic data. It has expanded to include guidance and data format specifications for various biometric modalities, including facial, iris, plantar, and DNA data. As the number of modalities and the complexity of the information have increased over time, the specification has grown to exceed 600 pages. Traditionally, software developers and system integrators have used this standard as a text-based reference, manually extracting and interpreting technical requirements to develop conformant software.

The ANSI/NIST-ITL 1 standards have historically required extensive cross-referencing within the document. Requirements for a single data element (e.g., data type, character constraints, occurrence limits) are often distributed and repeated across narrative sections and associated tables. This fragmentation has increased the risk of ambiguity when separate sections present inconsistent or conflicting guidance, particularly in a long and complex technical specification maintained over multiple revisions. Organizations have therefore had to reconcile related requirements before implementing them, and independent reconciliation efforts could lead to divergent interpretations and subtle interoperability challenges.

NIST developed the Biometric Conformance Test Software (BioCTS) to validate whether implementations conform to the standard. BioCTS is valuable, but it is primarily a reactive tool — it identifies nonconformance after implementation work has begun. It does not negate the need to interpret requirements before design and development, nor does it prevent misunderstandings from being built into an implementation.

Before this NIST-led effort, an external initiative created “Machine-Readable Tables” for the 2011 and 2013 revisions. Those spreadsheet-based tables used proprietary software to generate XML representations of the standard’s requirements. The resources were not maintained and had limited industry adoption, so most organizations have continued to extract requirements independently from the narrative text.

This report describes NIST’s development of a machine-readable specification (MRS) for ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025. The MRS represents requirements from the text standard as structured JSON data. JSON was selected because it can represent the standard’s hierarchy (e.g., transactions, records, fields, subfields, information items) in a form that software can validate, transform, and use directly. The MRS is intended to supplement the human-readable standard.

The scope of this report covers the process used for extracting requirements for transactions, records, fields, subfields, and information items and codifying them into a structured JSON format. This document also provides a technical overview of the supporting infrastructure, including the strongly typed JSON schema and the suite of Python scripts developed to aggregate, validate, and transform the MRS data. Furthermore, the report describes the workflow batch script used to ensure consistent, repeatable validation and the generation of a proof-of-concept HTML output page. This generated output demonstrates that the machine-readable data can accurately recreate human-readable requirements while remaining accessible to automated tools. Finally, this report outlines the strategy for releasing the project as an open-source resource. It describes how making the entirety of the effort publicly available is intended to foster a collaborative environment in which the biometric community can provide feedback, submit fixes, and contribute to the maintenance of the MRS.
The remainder of this report proceeds from data modeling to implementation:
Section 2 describes how requirements are represented in JSON.
Section 3 describes the build and validation process.
Section 4 explains how generated HTML is used to review the JSON representation.

Organizations worldwide rely on the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1 standard, including the International Criminal Police Organization (INTERPOL), the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The 2025 revision reduced the cross-reference burden for readers by placing related data specifications closer to the narrative requirements that describe them rather than distributing those details across many sections. It also resolved inconsistencies between the requirements represented in different sections of the text (e.g., within text clauses, tables, and figures).

NIST developed a JSON-encoded version of ANSI/NIST-ITL 1 to provide the global community with a single shared interpretation of the standard’s complex requirements. The MRS facilitates rapid, consistent, and accurate deployments of the standard across varied technical environments and supports the exchange and integrity of biometric and forensic transactions. It can be used directly by software and adapted into implementation profiles to help minimize interoperability issues between organizations, ensure that disparate systems remain consistent and reduce the resource-intensive nature of manual requirement extraction. This will also enable NIST and the biometric community to manage the complexity of biometric data format requirements with greater agility, including simplified auditing and the integration of community contributions (e.g., corrections, enhancements). By providing a consistent digital reference, this machine-readable representation can be reliably deployed across multiple organizations to support the implementation of the standard.

NIST developed the MRS iteratively by extracting requirements from the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 text and subsequently expanding the schema to represent new requirement patterns. When a schema feature simplified an existing representation, previously encoded JSON data was revised to use the improved structure. This approach kept the final MRS consistent across the specification.

The JSON schema establishes a hierarchy that mirrors the organization of the standard, converting text-based requirements into reusable, tokenized data structures. The schema makes use of reusable components to define data (a subset can be found in Appendix A.1 in Fig. 6 and Fig. 7) and provides formal definitions for each data level to maintain structural consistency with the base standard, as seen in Table 1.

This modularity extends to data validation through a shared pattern library that houses regular expressions in a single location. By referencing these patterns throughout the MRS, the schema ensures that validation logic is applied consistently without repeating complex patterns for every instance.
The common structural elements mapped within the MRS are illustrated in Fig. 1:
Identifier — Typically a record type number, a combination of a record type number and field number, or another unique identifier
Mnemonic — A shorthand character string (typically 3-7 characters) used to identify fields and information items
Field name — The full, formal title of the data element, as defined in the standard
Description — The full textual description of the data, retained to serve as a human-readable reference within the machine-readable specification
Condition — Specifies whether the data is mandatory, optional, or user-defined, often incorporating conditional logic and encoding specific rules
Occurrence — Defines the number of times a data element may appear, ranging from fixed counts to dynamic values governed by conditional logic
Value Constraints — Specifies allowed values, ranges, or references to external tables, often using complex conditional logic to express requirements

Beyond structural mirroring, the JSON schema incorporates a logic-handling system to manage the standard’s complex requirements. It uses specialized definitions for condition and occurrence types that allow for encoding specific rules. For example, a field may be mandatory in a traditional encoding but optional in a National Information Exchange Model (NIEM) (i.e., XML-based) encoding. These logic structures (including predicates, outcomes, and Boolean operations; see Appendix A.2) are integrated directly into the data elements. This enables the representation of conditional dependencies, where the requirements for a specific field are contingent upon the value of a separate data element. For example, the Value Constraints for field 8.006 (seen at the bottom of Fig. 1) are governed by the value of the Scan Resolution Table (SRT) field. In this example, SRT values 0 and 1 require field 8.006 to contain an integer from 10 to 65535, while SRT value 2 requires the field value to be 0. By breaking down text-based requirements into these discrete, formal components, the JSON specification provides a machine-verifiable mechanism for enforcing complex data constraints that are found throughout the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 standard.
3. Structured Data Development and Software Build Process

NIST developed a strongly typed JSON schema and a suite of Python scripts to aggregate, validate, and transform the data in the MRS. Python was selected for this effort because of its widespread availability across numerous platforms as well as its extensive and mature libraries for JSON processing and data validation. This ensures that the tools remain accessible to the biometric community and can effectively manage the structural complexities of the MRS.

The MRS is maintained as modular partial JSON files rather than as one monolithic document. The complete MRS is nearly 120,000 lines, and a single file proved difficult to edit in common development environments. The partial files are development modules; the build process assembles them into a complete JSON document for validation and publication. This modular structure also supports implementation profiles that include only records, fields, or other data relevant to a specific deployment.

At a high level, the batch script performs four steps: it merges the partial JSON files, validates the combined file against the schema, transforms the validated data into HTML, and post-processes the generated HTML for review. Fig. 3 shows output from this automated workflow.

The validation step checks that the combined JSON is syntactically valid and conforms to the schema. If an error occurs during validation, the Python script identifies the most relevant error match and generates a human-readable “friendly path” to the violation. This logic replaces the generic built-in data element and array indexes with descriptive labels pulled directly from the JSON data (e.g., a specific record type, field name) to help developers pinpoint and resolve mismatches more efficiently.
After successful validation, a transformation script generates an HTML representation of the standard directly from the JSON source, as illustrated in Fig. 4.

The script identifies references to record types, field numbers, information items, and tables and automatically applies hyperlinks to the output. This tagging improves navigation and demonstrates how the structured data can support additional forms of document automation. A final post-processing utility cleans up the HTML markup to produce an auditable, human-readable technical document from the validated JSON data.
4. Generated HTML Specification and Data Verification

The automated generation of the HTML specification serves as the primary proof-of-concept for the MRS by testing whether the data model can support reconstruction of the standard’s requirements. To ensure a rigorous test, the transformation script is isolated from external narrative sources and relies exclusively on the JSON-encoded data to prevent the script from filling gaps with outside text. The resulting HTML document is a direct product of the information stored within the JSON. The successful reconstruction of complex biometric record types provides evidence that the JSON schema and data structures capture the specifications of the ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 standard without omitting critical details.
Fig. 5 shows the HTML representation for field 8.006, which can be compared to the original ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 text-based specification in Fig. 1.

This comparison demonstrates that the requirements for field 8.006 have been captured in the JSON and reproduced in the generated HTML. Similar comparisons across record types can be used to review coverage across the complete MRS.

To encourage adoption and keep the MRS current, NIST is releasing the project as an open-source repository. This public repository will allow users to propose corrections, report issues, and suggest enhancements. Users may also copy the repository for internal use. Changes to the NIST-maintained version, however, must pass schema validation and subject-matter review before incorporation.

The automated validation scripts serve as an initial technical filter to ensure that any proposed update is structured correctly, follows the schema, and can complete the entire build process. A successful build only confirms that the data is well-formed; it does not mean a change will be accepted. While expert review and technical consensus remain necessary, using the JSON data and the automated build process allows any tool or transformation that uses the MRS to reflect updates as soon as they are approved and incorporated.

The MRS for ANSI/NIST-ITL 1-2025 translates text-based biometric data exchange requirements into structured JSON. By converting more than 600 pages of requirements into machine-processable data, NIST has reduced the need for manual extraction and lowered the risk of inconsistent interpretation. This project uses modular JSON files, a JSON schema, and automated build scripts to assemble and validate the MRS. NIST expert review remains necessary to ensure that the JSON accurately represents the base standard.

Together, the schema, validation scripts, generated HTML output, and expert review process establish a repeatable workflow for maintaining the MRS as a technical resource and community-supported reference. The resulting JSON data can support implementation, testing, and auditing tools while preserving NIST review of the official specification.
